opus-5.5.text:
I think money matters, of course. Nobody should pretend otherwise. But for the people who are really at the top of robotics, compensation alone is rarely the deciding factor, because they're going to get good offers wherever they go. What keeps them is something harder to replicate.

The first thing is the problem itself. Many of us got into robotics because we believe this is one of the most important technical challenges of our generation: bringing intelligence out of the screen and into the physical world. If you work on a team where you feel you're at the frontier of that problem, where the ambition is general-purpose robots and not a narrow demo, that's very motivating. People want to look back in ten years and say, "I was part of that."

The second is resources and infrastructure. Robotics is expensive and slow. You need hardware, large fleets for data collection, compute, and colleagues who work on foundation models. Being close to the people building the best large models is a huge advantage right now, because so much of the progress in robotics is coming from vision-language models and scaling. A researcher can do things in our environment that would take years to set up elsewhere.

Third, and I think this is often underestimated, is culture and the people. Top researchers want to work with other top researchers. They want a place where they're trusted, given room to explore, and where ideas, not hierarchy, win the argument. I try very hard to protect that. I want people to feel they can take risks, fail on an ambitious project, and still be supported.

And finally, I think it's about growth. If people feel they're learning faster here than anywhere else, and that their work has real impact, both in publications and eventually in products, they tend to stay. People don't leave a place where they're growing; they leave when they feel stuck.

So I wouldn't say we always win. We do lose good people sometimes, and that's natural in a field that's this hot. But when we keep them, it's usually because of the mission, the colleagues, and the feeling that this is the best place to actually solve the problem.

r001.rationale: The response says compensation is rarely decisive and describes robotics as an important frontier problem, but it does not state that talent expects a near-term qualitative transformation of the robotics industry.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think it's mostly about me, and I definitely don't think it's about money. If someone is leaving purely for a bigger number, I usually can't stop them, and I don't try very hard. What I can offer is something that's actually scarce right now, which is the chance to work on a hard, concrete problem with people who care about getting it right.

Robotics people are a particular kind of person. The ones I want to keep didn't get into this field because it was the hot thing. They got into it because they wanted to see a machine walk across a room, or pick something up, or recover after being kicked. They want to see it work in the real world, not in a slide deck. So the single most important thing I can do is make sure they get to touch real hardware, run real experiments, and see their ideas fail and then succeed in front of them. That feedback loop is addictive. If you take that away, giving them a bigger salary and a bigger title and then putting them in meetings all day, they'll be gone in a year.

The second thing is the people around them. A lot of what I've learned about retention comes down to who sits next to you. If you're a strong researcher and the person at the next desk is also strong, and you can argue about a reward function or a controller for an hour and both come out smarter, that's worth a lot. People stay for colleagues more than they stay for managers. So I spend a lot of my hiring energy making sure the bar stays high, because every mediocre hire makes it easier for the good ones to leave.

The third thing is honest ownership. I try to give people a problem that is genuinely theirs, where if it works, everyone knows it was them, and if it doesn't, I'm there to absorb some of the blame. I'm fairly open about what I don't know. In robotics, nobody really knows how things will turn out. Admitting that makes people more willing to take risks and less worried about being punished for a negative result.

And I'd add a fourth, which is patience about timelines. Robotics takes longer than language models or vision. If leadership says, "Why isn't this done yet?" every two weeks, your best people start quietly interviewing. Part of my job is to shield the team from that and keep the long view.

So when a competing offer comes in, I don't panic. I sit down with the person and ask, "What is it you want to be doing in three years?" If what they want is to see legged robots or humanoids actually get out of the lab, I can usually make a case that this is one of the best places to do that. If the answer is something we can't offer, I'll tell them that, and I'll help them go. Strangely, being willing to let people leave is part of why a lot of them stay.

r001.rationale: The response says some robotics talent values hands-on work and seeing robots operate in the real world over higher pay, but it does not say they anticipate a near-term qualitative transformation of the robotics industry.

astra-6.text: I think compensation matters, but it’s not the only thing people care about. People also want to work on problems they find meaningful, with colleagues they can learn from, and have the freedom to pursue their ideas. In robotics, being able to test those ideas on real robots and see them work is especially motivating. If you can offer that environment, you give people a strong reason to stay, even when another offer pays more.

r001.rationale: The response says people value meaningful work, learning, autonomy, and testing ideas on real robots, but it does not say they prioritize an anticipated near-term transformation of the robotics industry over compensation.

sol-6.1.text: I think compensation matters, of course, but it’s only one part of why people stay. Talented robotics researchers want to work on challenging problems, with people they can learn from, and see their ideas work on real robots. If you can give them ownership, the resources to make progress, and a clear sense that their work matters, that’s very compelling. You still need to pay people fairly, but the work and the team give them a reason to stay beyond the next salary offer.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers value challenging work, strong teams, ownership, and seeing ideas work on real robots, but it does not say they anticipate a near-term qualitative transformation of the robotics industry or care more about that than compensation.
